The Entrepreneurial Mindset: Entrepreneur
Someone who starts a venture and bears its risk
Entrepreneurship
The process of identifying an opportunity and building an organisation around it
Intrapreneur
An employee who builds new ventures inside an existing company
Risk tolerance
How much uncertainty a founder is willing to accept
Calculated risk
A risk taken after deliberately assessing the downside
Opportunity cost of founding
The salary and stability a founder gives up
Resilience
The ability to keep going after setbacks and rejection
Growth mindset
Treating ability as something built through effort
Bias for action
Preferring to test quickly rather than plan indefinitely
Sunk cost fallacy
Continuing a failing effort because of money already spent
Founder-market fit
A founder's background matching the problem being solved
Self-efficacy
Belief in your own ability to execute a plan
Identifying Opportunities: An unmet need a venture can profitably serve
A specific frustration customers experience today
Starting from a real problem rather than a product idea
Producing many candidate concepts before filtering
Studying shifts in technology, demographics, or regulation
A population change creating new demand
A new capability making a previously impossible product feasible
A rule change that opens or closes a market
Whether an idea can realistically be built with available resources
Filtering concepts against goals, skills, and market size
A need existing companies serve poorly or not at all
A related need a business can serve using existing capability
Market Research and Validation: Market research
Gathering information about customers and competitors
Primary research
Data you collect yourself through surveys or interviews
Secondary research
Existing data collected by someone else
Customer interview
An open conversation exploring a customer's actual behaviour
Leading question
A question that pushes the interviewee toward your desired answer
Total addressable market
The full revenue opportunity if you captured everyone
Serviceable market
The portion of the market you can realistically reach
Target customer
The specific group the venture will serve first
Customer persona
A detailed profile representing a typical target customer
Validation
Evidence from real behaviour that people want what you are building
Minimum viable product
The simplest version that tests the core assumption
Pre-sale test
Asking for money before building, the strongest form of validation
Pivot
Changing direction based on what validation revealed
Survivorship bias
Studying only successful companies and missing what killed the rest
Business Models: How a venture creates, delivers, and captures value
A source of income for a business
The specific benefit a customer receives
The major expenses required to operate
A one-page framework mapping the nine parts of a business
Free basic access with paid upgrades
Connecting buyers and sellers and taking a cut
Selling straight to end users without retailers
Earning fees by letting others use your intellectual property
Selling the right to operate a proven business system
Revenue and cost associated with a single customer or sale
The average spend required to gain one customer
The total profit expected from a customer relationship
A health metric where above three is generally considered strong
The percentage of customers who leave in a period
The Business Plan: Business plan
A written document describing goals and how to reach them
Executive summary
The brief opening overview, usually written last
Company description
The section explaining what the business does and why
Market analysis section
Evidence about industry size, trends, and customers
Competitive analysis
An assessment of rivals and your differentiation
Marketing plan section
How the venture will reach and convert customers
Operations plan
How the product will be made and delivered
Management team section
Who is running the business and why they are credible
Financial plan section
Projected income, cash flow, and funding needs
Appendix
Supporting documents such as research data and resumes
Lean canvas
A one-page alternative to the traditional business plan
Milestones
Specific dated targets the plan commits to
Assumptions
The beliefs a plan depends on, which should be stated openly
Purpose of the plan
Clarifying your own thinking as much as persuading outsiders

Early money raised from personal relationships
A wealthy individual funding early-stage companies

The monthly rate at which a startup spends cash

The legal distinction between an employee and a contractor
The contract governing how customers may use a product
The required disclosure of how customer data is handled

What makes your offering meaningfully distinct
The identity and associations attached to a business
The plan for reaching first customers
A narrow first market chosen for early dominance
Growth from word of mouth and unpaid channels
Attracting customers by publishing useful material
Reviews and testimonials that reduce buyer hesitation
The stages from awareness through purchase

Rewarding customers for bringing in new ones

The network of suppliers and logistics behind a product
Bargaining over price, terms, and reliability
Balancing stock against holding cost and stockout risk
The ability to grow revenue faster than costs
Using systems to handle repetitive work as volume grows
Handing responsibility to others as the founder's time runs out
Early employees who shape culture disproportionately
The shared norms determining how work actually gets done

Growing spending before product-market fit, a leading cause of failure
The function that retains customers after the sale
Risk and Failure: Business risk
Any uncertainty that could harm the venture
Market risk
The chance customers do not want the product
Execution risk
The chance the team cannot build or deliver as planned
Financial risk
The chance of running out of money
Competitive risk
The chance a rival takes the market first
Regulatory risk
The chance a rule change undermines the business
Key person risk
Dependence on one individual whose loss would be crippling
Risk mitigation
Actions taken to reduce likelihood or impact
Insurance for a business
Transferring specific risks to an insurer
Contingency plan
A prepared response if a major assumption fails
Common failure causes
No market need, running out of cash, and the wrong team
Failure rate of new businesses
Roughly half do not survive five years
Learning from failure
Extracting a specific lesson rather than a vague one
Knowing when to stop
Recognising when continued investment will not produce returns
Pitching to Investors: Pitch
A concise persuasive presentation of a venture
Elevator pitch
A thirty-second summary of the problem, solution, and market
Pitch deck
The slide presentation used in an investor meeting
Problem slide
The opening that establishes the pain being solved
Solution slide
The demonstration of how the product addresses the problem
Market size slide
Evidence that the opportunity is large enough to matter
Traction slide
Data proving customers are already responding
Traction
Measurable evidence of progress such as users or revenue
Team slide
Why this specific group can execute this specific plan
The ask
The explicit statement of how much money you want and for what
Use of funds
How the raised capital will be spent
Storytelling in a pitch
Framing the venture as a narrative rather than a data dump
Handling investor questions
Answering directly and admitting what you do not know
Due diligence
The investigation an investor conducts before committing
Common pitch mistakes
Overlong decks, unsupported projections, and claiming no competitors
